content.text:
Checkpoint 6 — React Inventory + Search.

Please review the existing React/Vite/TypeScript frontend and the completed backend frame APIs before making changes.

Build the main inventory screen with:

- inventory table using GET /api/frames
- backend pagination
- free-text search using q
- filters for status, mediaType, environment, format and region
- loading state
- API error state
- empty-results state
- useful columns from FrameSummaryResponse
- styling aligned with the supplied design system where practical

Keep this checkpoint limited to inventory/search only.

Do not implement:
- add frame
- edit frame
- history UI
- CSV import UI

Keep the frontend simple and suitable for a take-home exercise. Avoid unnecessary libraries and over-engineering.

Before changing files, inspect the current frontend structure and backend API contract and propose:

1. component structure
2. API/client approach
3. table columns
4. search/filter behaviour
5. pagination behaviour
6. files to add/change

Do not modify files yet. I want to review the approach first.

I’ll inspect the repository structure and the backend frame contract first, then trace the existing React/Vite conventions and design-system styles. I’ll return only a concrete implementation proposal—no file changes.

The frontend is currently a very small Vite starter, while the backend already has dedicated summary, criteria, and paged-response DTOs. I’m now reading those contracts alongside the controller tests and supplied design-system assets so the proposal matches actual parameter names, response shape, and established visual tokens.

The API contract is clear: filters are case-insensitive exact matches, while `q` is a case-insensitive contains search over frame ID, address, town, station, airport, and site number. Pagination is zero-based, defaults to 20, and sorting defaults to most recently modified with a stable frame-ID tie-breaker. I’m doing one final pass over the prototype’s inventory table, filters, tokens, and responsive styling before fixing the proposed UI shape.

I reviewed the frontend, backend search contract, integration tests, legacy CSV, and supplied design system. No files were modified.

The frontend is currently the minimal Vite health-check screen with only React 19. The existing Vite `/api` proxy can be reused unchanged.

## 1. Component structure

```text
App
└── AppShell
    └── InventoryPage
        ├── FrameFilters
        ├── InventoryTable
        │   └── StatusChip
        ├── Pagination
        └── Loading / Error / Empty state
```

State and fetching can remain in `InventoryPage`; a custom state-management library or router would be unnecessary.

## 2. API/client approach

Add a small typed client:

```ts
getFrames({
  page,
  size,
  q,
  status,
  mediaType,
  environment,
  format,
  region,
  signal,
})
```

It will:

- Call `GET /api/frames`.
- Include only non-empty query parameters.
- Keep the backend’s default `modifiedDate,desc` ordering.
- Model `FrameSummaryResponse`, `FramePageResponse`, and RFC Problem Details.
- Parse useful API error messages.
- Accept an `AbortSignal` so superseded searches do not update the UI.
- Use plain `fetch`; no additional dependencies.

## 3. Table columns

A compact table using only summary-response data:

- Frame ID
- Site — station or airport, with address beneath
- Location — town with region beneath
- Media type
- Format
- Environment
- Status — design-system-style chip
- Last updated — locally formatted `modifiedDate`

Null values will render as an em dash. Rows will not link to details or expose edit/history actions in this checkpoint.

## 4. Search/filter behaviour

- One prominent search input mapped to `q`.
- Debounce free-text search by roughly 300 ms.
- Reset to page 1 whenever search or a filter changes.
- Status, media type, environment, format, and region are single-value filters because the backend accepts one exact value for each.
- Filters are case-insensitive exact matches; search is a case-insensitive substring match.
- Search covers the backend-supported fields: frame ID, address, town, station, airport, and site number.
- Provide “Clear filters” when anything is active.

The API currently has no facet/options endpoint. I propose native inputs with `datalist` suggestions based on the supplied inventory values. This avoids pretending the known CSV values are a closed enum while still making common values easy to select.

## 5. Pagination behaviour

- Backend-driven, zero-based requests with user-facing one-based page labels.
- Default page size: 20.
- Rows-per-page choices: 20, 50, and 100.
- Previous/next controls disabled at the boundaries and during requests.
- Display `Showing X–Y of Z`.
- Reset to the first page when page size changes.
- If refreshed data makes the current page invalid, return to the last valid page.

## 6. Files to add/change

Change:

- `src/App.tsx` — render the inventory application.
- `src/App.css` — inventory layout and component styling.
- `src/index.css` — reset, typography, and global design-system setup.

Add:

- `src/api/frames.ts` — request construction, response types, and error handling.
- `src/components/AppShell.tsx`
- `src/components/FrameFilters.tsx`
- `src/components/FrameTable.tsx`
- `src/components/Pagination.tsx`
- `src/styles/tokens.css` — production subset copied from the supplied source-of-truth tokens.
- Inter font assets copied from the supplied design system.

The shell will use the design system’s near-white canvas, dark inventory rail, Inter typography, blue focus/action colour, bordered surfaces, dense table spacing, and restrained status colours. It will omit inactive add/import/edit/history affordances and prototype-only controls such as map view, column selection, saved searches, and bulk selection.

I reviewed the Checkpoint 6 proposal. Please proceed with implementation using these final decisions.

ACCEPT:
- Keep the proposed component structure: InventoryPage, FrameFilters, FrameTable, Pagination and UI states.
- Use plain fetch with a small typed API client.
- Reuse the existing Vite /api proxy.
- Keep state and fetching in InventoryPage; no state-management library or router.
- Use backend pagination with page sizes 20, 50 and 100.
- Use q for debounced free-text search and reset to page 1 when search/filter/page size changes.
- Support loading, API error and empty-result states.
- Keep the proposed inventory table columns.
- Use the supplied design-system styles/tokens where practical.
- Keep this checkpoint limited to inventory/search/filter/pagination.

CHANGE:
- Status should be a dropdown because the supported UI values are LIVE and INACTIVE.
- For the inventory filter use:
  All
  LIVE
  INACTIVE
- Later, for Add/Edit Frame, status will also be a LIVE/INACTIVE dropdown and LIVE should be the default for a new frame. Do not implement Add/Edit now.
- Keep mediaType, environment, format and region as simple string-based filter controls using the existing backend query parameters.

REJECT:
- Do not assume or introduce backend FrameStatus or FrameType enums. The current backend fields are Strings.
- Do not create CSV-derived pseudo-enums or hard-code dropdown options for mediaType, environment, format or region.
- Do not add a new backend filter-options/facets API.
- Do not change the backend model/API for this checkpoint.
- Do not add @CrossOrigin or other CORS changes; use the existing Vite proxy.
- Do not copy/add font files unless already required by the starter.
- Do not add router, state-management libraries or unnecessary dependencies.
- Do not implement Add/Edit, History or CSV Import UI yet.

Please implement Checkpoint 6 now.

After implementation:
1. run the frontend tests if present,
2. run the production build,
3. report the files changed,
4. summarize the implemented behaviour,
5. report any MUST FIX or SHOULD FIX findings.

Keep the implementation simple and production-minded without over-engineering.

I’ll implement the approved inventory-only slice now. I’ll keep the non-status filters as unrestricted string inputs, use only `LIVE`/`INACTIVE` in the status dropdown, and preserve the backend’s string contract throughout. Afterward I’ll run the available frontend checks and production build.

The implementation is now being applied in small, reviewable files: the API boundary, page state, filters, table, pagination, and shell remain separate. The first patch needed splitting because the patch tool does not allow replacing a file via delete-and-add in one operation; no repository content was changed by that failed attempt.

content.text: The inventory flow is implemented: typed `GET /api/frames` calls, abortable/debounced searching, exact string filters, the requested status dropdown, server pagination, table rendering, retryable errors, and distinct empty states. I’m at the verification pass now, including TypeScript/build feedback and a focused review for request-state edge cases.

The source checks could not start because the frontend dependencies are not installed (`eslint` and `tsc` are absent from `node_modules`). I’m installing the lockfile-pinned dependencies, then I’ll rerun lint and the production build. No test script is currently defined in `package.json`.

The production build already passes. Lint identified one React 19 rule violation: request-state flags were being set synchronously inside the fetch effect. I’m moving those transitions to the user actions that initiate requests, leaving the effect responsible only for synchronizing with the API.

Show me where GET /api/frames is called and explain how search, filters, page and size become query parameters.
I’ll point to the exact client call and the page state that supplies each parameter.

The request originates in [InventoryPage.tsx](D:\Global\frame-inventory-exercise-main\src\frontend\src\components\InventoryPage.tsx:32):

```ts
getFrames({ page, size, q: query, ...filters }, controller.signal)
```

The actual HTTP call is in [frames.ts](D:\Global\frame-inventory-exercise-main\src\frontend\src\api\frames.ts:44):

```ts
const searchParams = new URLSearchParams({
  page: String(params.page),
  size: String(params.size),
})

addIfPresent(searchParams, 'q', params.q)
addIfPresent(searchParams, 'status', params.status)
addIfPresent(searchParams, 'mediaType', params.mediaType)
addIfPresent(searchParams, 'environment', params.environment)
addIfPresent(searchParams, 'format', params.format)
addIfPresent(searchParams, 'region', params.region)

fetch(`/api/frames?${searchParams.toString()}`, ...)
```

`page` and `size` are always included. Search and filters are trimmed and included only when non-empty by `addIfPresent()`.

For example:

```text
/api/frames?page=0&size=20&q=station&status=LIVE&region=London
```

State behaviour:

- Search input is debounced for 300 ms, trimmed, then assigned to `q`.
- Changing search or any filter resets `page` to `0`.
- Pagination changes `page`.
- Rows-per-page changes `size` and resets `page` to `0`.
- `URLSearchParams` handles URL encoding automatically.
Explain exactly how the 300ms search debounce works in our current code, with one example of typing "London".

In `InventoryPage.tsx`, `queryInput` updates immediately on every keystroke. This effect watches it:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  const timeout = window.setTimeout(() => {
    setLoading(true)
    setError(null)
    setPage(0)
    setQuery(queryInput.trim())
  }, 300)

  return () => window.clearTimeout(timeout)
}, [queryInput])
```

Typing “London”:

- Type `L`: starts a 300 ms timer.
- Type `o` before it expires: React cleanup cancels the `L` timer and starts another.
- The same happens for `n`, `d`, `o`, and `n`.
- After the final `n`, if nothing changes for 300 ms, the callback runs.
- It trims the text, resets pagination to page `0`, and sets `query` to `"London"`.
- Because the API effect watches `query`, it then calls:

```text
GET /api/frames?page=0&size=20&q=London
```

Thus, no search request is made for each intermediate value such as `Lond`; only the settled value is submitted. The normal initial inventory request still runs when the page first loads.

I’ll review the changed frontend as-is, without editing. I’m tracing the state transitions through mount, debounce, filter changes, pagination, retry, abort cleanup, and out-of-order responses, then checking the rendered semantics and responsive layout.

## MUST FIX

1. Loading can become permanently stuck without an API request.  
   [InventoryPage.tsx:20](D:\Global\frame-inventory-exercise-main\src\frontend\src\components\InventoryPage.tsx:20) sets `loading=true` when the debounce expires, even if trimmed `query`, `page`, and filters have not changed. This occurs on initial mount when the first request finishes within 300 ms, when adding/removing whitespace, or when clearing an uncommitted search. Since the fetch effect dependencies remain unchanged, no request runs to restore `loading=false`.

## SHOULD FIX

1. Page correction can report the wrong loading state.  
   [InventoryPage.tsx:34](D:\Global\frame-inventory-exercise-main\src\frontend\src\components\InventoryPage.tsx:34) changes an out-of-range page, but the previous request’s `finally` can set `loading=false` before the corrected-page request finishes. Loading should be tied to the active request rather than duplicated across event handlers.

2. Exact string filters request on every keystroke.

Yes, exactly.

`loading=true` is set when the debounce timer fires, but React only runs the API effect if `query`, `page`, or filters actually changed. If they did not change, no request runs and nothing resets `loading` to `false`.

Make loading state controlled by the actual active/latest API request.
Do not set loading=true from debounce, filter, pagination, or other event handlers when an API request may not actually occur.
Ensure loading cannot remain stuck when the effective query/filter values do not change.

2. SHOULD FIX — Page correction loading race
Handle this together with #1.
If an out-of-range page is corrected and triggers another request, an older request must not set loading=false while the newer request is still running.
Only the active/latest request should control the final loading state.

3. SHOULD FIX — String filters request on every keystroke
Apply the same ~300 ms debounce pattern used by q search to the free-text filters:
- mediaType
- environment

Keep the existing pagination behaviour unchanged.
